question: How cheaply can an attacker produce peer IDs closer to a chosen key than the entire honest network?
transcription_note: Values transcribed from stdout. The CLI has no --json output yet; adding one is the next task, and until then these records are hand-copied rather than machine-emitted.

environment.host: Intel Xeon @ 2.10GHz, 2 vCPU (cloud container, not a fast machine)
environment.note: rust-toolchain.toml pins 1.98.1; this run used 1.95.0. Re-run on the pinned toolchain before citing externally.

honest_baseline.source: ProbeLab weekly crawl — unique peer IDs discovered
honest_baseline.derivation: For N uniformly distributed IDs, the number with CPL >= j to a random target is N * 2^-j. Closest: j = log2(N). 20th closest: j = log2(N/20).

finding: At 1.6 seconds of single-core time, the best ground identity reaches CPL 17 against an honest network whose closest peer sits at CPL ~13.5. Roughly two seconds of laptop CPU beats the placement of every peer in the Amino DHT for a chosen key. Each 10x increase in trials buys about 2 more bits.
caveats: best_cpl is the single closest identity. The CLI truncates output at 5 entries, so the worst of the kept 20 was not recorded; the claim that ALL 20 beat the honest 20th-closest (CPL ~9.1) is strongly implied by the margin but is not yet measured. Fix with --json output.
Single-threaded. Grinding is embarrassingly parallel, so a real attacker multiplies this by core count and again by renting machines.
Each run is a single sample of a maximum, so best_cpl has meaningful variance. Repeat n>=10 before quoting a precise figure.
Honest baseline is analytic, not measured from a crawl. Phase 2 replaces it with real data.
